About this document


This document provides the teaching content for English as an Additional Language
Stages 1–5 of the New Zealand Curriculum.

Progress and assessment information for English as an Additional Language Stages
1–5 is still in development. Once that is completed, English as an Additional
Language Stages 1–5 is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as a
National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training
Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer English as an Additional Language Stages 1–5 will be required to start
using it in Year 11 from 1 January 2028, in Year 12 from 1 January 2029, and in Year
13 from 1 January 2030.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

The curriculum is organised in five stages. Post-beginner English language learners
enter at the stage appropriate to their current language level. EAL Stage 1 assumes a
foundational level of English with a firm knowledge of grapheme–phoneme
correspondence. Schools may need to provide intensive and additional English
Language support, including structured literacy, to students who do not yet have the
required language level to access this curriculum.
At Stage 1, students are taught fundamental language skills through engaging with
and crafting simple texts, partaking in everyday conversations, and listening to
simple, familiar English. They are taught increasingly complex language features, text
types, and ideas until, by Stage 5, they draw on the knowledge and practices of
English to examine issues, communicate viewpoints, and engage with the world
around them. They are taught to create written and spoken texts tailored to specific
audiences and purposes and to communicate with increasing accuracy,
appropriateness, confidence, and independence.

requires five to seven years and potentially up to 10 for certain learners (Baker and

Across Stages 1–5, students develop receptive and productive skills, building on their
linguistic knowledge and understanding of different text types, audiences, purposes,
and appropriate language features. Learning progresses through increasing
complexity, independence, and confidence in communicating. Receptive skills
support comprehension and interpretation of language, while productive skills enable
meaningful communication across a range of contexts. Language acquisition is most
effective when receptive and productive skills are integrated throughout the teaching
and learning programme. Students should be exposed to a variety of text types to
model functions, features, and conventions across the curriculum. Students should
have access to engaging and relevant content so they can partake in extensive
reading and listening outside the classroom.

Language learning is a gradual, long-term process that develops through ongoing
practice and exposure. Progress is supported when learners take risks and recognise
that making mistakes is a natural and valuable part of acquiring a new language. A
collaborative and supportive learning environment further strengthens this
development, enabling students to engage actively, build confidence, and grow their
language capabilities together.

                     Some words occur more frequently than others in spoken and written English. The most frequent words make up a large proportion              Communicate similar ideas using related words from the same word family.
                      of the words used in many texts and conversations.
                     Knowledge of the most frequent words supports comprehension and communication across a range of everyday topics and
                      situations.
                     Words consist of base words (e.g. teach) and prefixes and suffixes (types of affixes), which can be combined to create new words

                     Words in the same word family share a common base word; knowledge of word parts can help identify the base word and part of
                      speech (e.g. help = base word/verb; helper = noun; helpful = adjective; helpfully = adverb).
                     The most frequent word parts occur across many word families and can help to understand unfamiliar words (e.g. ‘speaker’,
                      ‘teacher’, and ‘computer’ are nouns formed from verbs with the prefix –er).

                    Describing, comparing, and quantifying                                                                                                        Describe people, places, things, experiences, and ideas by adding details about qualities, actions, and time.
                    Describing                                                                                                                                    Communicate similarities and differences between people, places, things, ideas, and experiences.
                     Adjectives can be used to add information about people, places, things, and ideas (e.g. This is a red car; the room is clean).              Express quantity, amount, and degree when sharing information.
                     When more than one adjective is used together, they usually appear in a predictable order (e.g. adjectives describing size usually          Add information about actions, qualities, and time to make meaning more precise.
                      come before those relating to colour: a big red car).                                                                                       Interpret and communicate descriptive and comparative information across a range of contexts.
                    Comparing
                     Comparisons between two people, things, or ideas can be made using specific word forms (comparative adjectives) and sentence
                      patterns. Typically, one-syllable adjectives add ‘–er + than’ (e.g. smaller than), and three-syllable adjectives use ‘more + adjective +
                      than’ (e.g. more expensive than). Two-syllable adjectives may follow either pattern (e.g. simpler, more simple).
                     Similarities between people, things, or ideas can be expressed using ‘as + adjective + as’ (e.g. My brother is as tall as me).
                     Groups of people, things, or ideas can be compared to identify the highest or lowest degree of a quality using specific word forms
                      (superlative adjectives) and sentence patterns. Typically, one-syllable adjectives use ‘the + adjective + –est’ (e.g. the tallest), and
                      three-syllable adjectives use ‘the most + adjective’ (e.g. the most expensive). Two-syllable adjective may follow either pattern.
                     When adding –er or –est, the final consonant is doubled (e.g. big → biggest).
                     When adding –er or –est to a word ending in ‘y’, the ‘y’ is changed to ‘i’ (e.g. happy → happier).
                    Adding information about actions, qualities, and time
                     Adverbs can be used to add information about verbs, adjectives, other adverbs, and whole sentences (e.g. She speaks clearly; The
                      test was quite easy; Sadly, we didn’t go).
                     Words like ‘too’ and ‘enough’ (adverbs of degree) express whether the amount/degree is right for what is needed (e.g. My bag is too
                      heavy; He isn’t old enough to drive).
                     Words like ‘now’, ‘today’, and ‘soon’ (adverbs of time) express when something happens (e.g. The bus will come soon).
                    Quantity and groups
                     Words like ‘many’, ‘much’, ‘a lot of’, ‘a few’, ‘a little’, ‘some’, and ‘any’ (quantifiers) tell us about quantity:
                      o ‘Many’, ‘a lot of’, and ‘a few’ are used with countable nouns (e.g. a few books)
                      o ‘Much’, and ‘a little’ are used with uncountable nouns (e.g. a little water)
                      o ‘Some’ and ‘any’ can be used with countable or uncountable nouns.

                    Additional detail
                     Phrases are groups of words that work together but do not form a complete sentence as they do not contain both a subject and a

                    Complete ideas
                     Clause are groups of words that contain a subject and a verb (e.g. She laughed).
                     An independent clause has a subject and a verb and is a complete sentence (e.g. I didn’t play netball).

                     A sentence expresses a complete idea. Sentences usually begin with a capital letter and end with a full stop, question mark, or

                    Combining ideas
                     A compound sentence is formed by joining two independent clauses that can each stand alone as a complete sentence (e.g. I like
                      football and my brother likes rugby).
                     The clauses in a compound sentence can be linked with the words ‘and’, ‘but’, and ‘so’ (e.g. I was tired, so I went to bed).
                     Commas are used to separate clauses in compound sentences before ‘and’, ‘but’, and ‘so’ (e.g. Hans speaks German, but he
                      doesn’t speak Spanish).
                     A comma is often used before the linking word in compound sentences (e.g. She likes rice, but I like noodles).
                    Speech and dialogue
                     Direct speech uses a person’s exact words in speech marks (e.g. ‘Hello,’ she said; She said, ‘Hi, my name is Yumiko’).
                     In written dialogue, a new line is usually used for each speaker.
                     Speech marks are used to show direct speech or dialogue.
